explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "…I did not come with eloquence or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the testimony about God." No fancy speech and no polished words. He still proclaimed the testimony about God, just without the polish.

Close, but Paul did preach. Verse 4 mentions "My message and my preaching…" So the preaching was there. What he says was missing was the eloquence and the wisdom. Plain delivery is still delivery, friend.
Paul says the opposite here. He came "…as I proclaimed to you the testimony about God." The testimony was part of what he brought. The things he says he did not come with were eloquence and wisdom.

explanations.answer: Nothing except Jesus Christ and Him crucified
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says, "…I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified." That was his resolve while he was with them. Jesus Christ, and Him crucified, is the focus he names.

explanations.answer: Nothing except the Law and the Prophets
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, but that's not what verse 2 says. Paul narrows his focus to one thing, "…Jesus Christ and Him crucified." The Law and the Prophets don't make the list in this verse. It's a short list, friend, and it has one name on it.

explanations.answer: Nothing except the wisdom of the Greeks
explanations.explanation: Not this time, baker. Paul says he did not come with eloquence or wisdom (verse 1), and he resolved to know nothing except Jesus Christ and Him crucified (verse 2). Greek wisdom isn't on his list. A one-item list leaves no room for extras.
True, baker. Paul says, "I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling." He doesn't dress it up. It's an honest thing to say about yourself, and I respect it.
It's actually true, baker. Paul says, "I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling." He's honest about how he came. Hearing it from him is kind of a relief.

explanations.answer: A demonstration of the Spirit's power
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul says his message and preaching were "…not with persuasive words of wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power…" The power wasn't his. It came with the message from the Spirit.
Good try, but verse 4 doesn't mention letters of any kind. It says the message came "…with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power…" No paperwork needed, friend. The Spirit's power was the proof.

Nope, baker. Paul says his message was "…not with persuasive words of wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power…" Philosophers aren't named in this verse. What he says came with his message was the Spirit's power.

Not quite, baker. Paul says the opposite in verse 5, that he wanted "…your faith would not rest on men’s wisdom, but on God’s power." Faith that rests on clever talk is only as strong as the talker. He wanted theirs resting on something much sturdier.

Right, baker. Paul wanted their faith "…not rest on men’s wisdom, but on God’s power." That's why he came without polished speech. If the faith rested on his talking, it would be a lot to put on one man. God's power can hold it.

Careful, baker, Paul says the opposite. He speaks wisdom among the mature, "…not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing." He has wisdom to give, but it comes from a different place. Verse 7 tells us it's God's wisdom.

You got it, baker. Paul says it is "…not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing." The ones he says are coming to nothing are the rulers of this age. The wisdom he speaks is of a different kind, the wisdom of God (verse 7).

Yes, baker. God's wisdom was something "…He destined for our glory before time began." Paul puts the destining before time began, and "before" is the word that fits. That's his timing, so I'll stick with it.
Not after, friend. Verse 7 says God destined this wisdom for our glory "…before time began." Time hadn't even started yet. That's about as early as early gets.
Almost, but "as" doesn't fit the verse. Paul says God destined it "…before time began." It wasn't set while the clock was already ticking. It was set before the clock existed.
That's it, baker. Paul says, "For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." The rulers of this age didn't understand God's wisdom. That's a heavy verse, so I'll just let it sit.

explanations.answer: Burned the scroll of the prophet
explanations.explanation: No scrolls go up in smoke in this passage, friend. Verse 8 says that if the rulers had understood, "…they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." That's the thing Paul names. It's a heavy one.

That's not what verse 8 says, baker. Paul's talking about the rulers of this age and says they "…would not have crucified the Lord of glory." if they'd understood. The Lord of glory is the One in view here. Paul isn't talking about himself in that line.

explanations.answer: God revealed it to us by the Spirit
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul says no eye has seen, no ear has heard and no heart has imagined what God has prepared (verse 9). Then he says, "But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit." It's a gift, friend, and we get to open it.

explanations.answer: We worked it out by careful study
explanations.explanation: Study is a good thing, baker, but that's not what Paul says here. He says, "But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit." It was shown to us, not figured out by us. That's the whole point of the verse.

explanations.answer: An angel explained it to us in a dream
explanations.explanation: That's a fun picture, but no angel or dream shows up in these verses. Paul says, "But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit." The Spirit is the one he names. Keep it simple, baker.

You got it, baker. Paul asks, "For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him?" Your thoughts stay in you unless you share them. Even my best ideas stay in here until I say them out loud.

Friends are wonderful, baker, but Paul doesn't name them here. He asks, "For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him?" The one he names is the man's own spirit. Friends aren't in that verse.
Not the elders, friend. Paul says nobody among men knows a man's thoughts "…except his own spirit within him?" That's just between you and your own spirit. The town council can stay out of it.

explanations.answer: So we may understand what God has freely given us
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul says we received the Spirit who is from God "…that we may understand what God has freely given us." Freely given means a gift. The Spirit helps us see what's been handed to us.

explanations.answer: So we can win every argument with the wise
explanations.explanation: Good try, but winning arguments isn't the reason Paul gives. He says it's "…that we may understand what God has freely given us." Understanding is the goal here, friend. Nobody's keeping score.

explanations.answer: So we will be praised by the rulers of this age
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Paul's reason is "…that we may understand what God has freely given us." Praise from the rulers of this age isn't a reason he gives. Understanding what God has given is the one he names.

Not this time, baker. Paul says, "…not in words taught us by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit…" The words came from the Spirit, not from human wisdom. Same gift, and the Spirit even helped with the wrapping.

Right, baker. Paul says he speaks "…not in words taught us by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit…" He expresses "…spiritual truths in spiritual words." The Spirit gave the truth and the words to go with it.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned." The natural man doesn't accept them, and that's how they look to him. Understanding takes the Spirit.
Not rules, friend. Paul says the things from the Spirit of God "…are foolishness to him…" That's how the natural man sees them. Rules never come up in this verse.

Nice try, baker, but legends aren't in the verse. Paul says the things of the Spirit of God "…are foolishness to him…" He doesn't accept them, and he can't understand them. They're "spiritually discerned."

That's right, baker. Paul says, "The spiritual man judges all things…" The spiritual man is the one who can discern spiritual things, which the natural man can't. That's quite a difference between those two.
Enduring is a good word, baker, but it's not the one Paul uses here. He says the spiritual man "…judges all things…" Endure sounds like gritting your teeth, and Paul is talking about discerning.
No fear in this verse, friend. Paul says, "The spiritual man judges all things…" That's discernment, not worry. He's not hiding under the counter.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is not subject to anyone’s judgment." Those are his words, and I'll leave them just as he wrote them. That's verse 15, friend.

It's true, baker. Paul says, "The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is not subject to anyone’s judgment." Verse 15 holds both halves together: the spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is not subject to anyone's judgment. So the statement on the card is just what Paul wrote, and that's why False misses.
You got it, baker. Paul says, "But we have the mind of Christ." Nobody can instruct the Lord, yet we have the mind of Christ. That's a gift to be grateful for, not something to brag about.
Moses is a fine name, baker, but he's not who Paul names here. Paul says, "But we have the mind of Christ." Christ is the one in this verse. It's his mind we have.
Not the wise, friend. Paul has been setting human wisdom aside this whole passage. He says, "But we have the mind of Christ." That's a better thing to have than any amount of cleverness.
